title.text:
Uncertainty,
samples and cause

objects.text: How sure can we be of a number from a sample, and when does a pattern mean that one thing caused another?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 4 of 24  |  Module A: Think with data
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session we described the data we hold. Today we ask how sure we can be. If you look at thirty orders, how far can their average sit from the truth?

We find out by simulating it in Google Sheets, with no code at all. We also look at correlation, at why two things that move together may have nothing to do with each other, and at the ways a sample can quietly mislead you.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain why a sample differs from the population it came from, and measure that difference with the standard error. You can run a Monte Carlo simulation with RAND in Google Sheets and read the sampling distribution it produces.

And you can read a Pearson correlation, say what it does not show, and name a confounder and two kinds of bias. There is no code today. Every formula is one you can type into a cell.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts
first, then a Google Sheets lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_2eb46d76.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the sheet. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 3 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures. After a ten minute break we open the Lakeside Mart workbook in Google Sheets for a forty-five minute lab.

You build a simulation of two hundred samples, read a correlation, and question a pattern. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A manager asks what a typical order is worth. Which statistic do you lead with, and what else do you give?
2.  What is a pivot table in SQL and in pandas?
3.  A bar chart makes a small gap between two branches look huge. What do you check first?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 3. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A manager asks what a typical order is worth. Which statistic do you lead with, and what else do you give?

A good answer is this. The median, 24,800 UGX, with the number of orders and the IQR. The mean, 49,931, is pulled up by a few large orders.

Question two. What is a pivot table in SQL and in pandas?

A good answer is this. A GROUP BY in SQL and groupby in pandas: group the records, then aggregate each group.

Question three. A bar chart makes a small gap between two branches look huge. What do you check first?

A good answer is this. Whether the vertical axis starts at zero. Cutting the base makes small gaps look large.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. For a typical order you lead with the median, 24,800 shillings, and give the number of orders and the IQR beside it, because a few very large orders pull the mean up to 49,931. A pivot table is a GROUP BY in SQL and groupby in pandas: you group the records, then aggregate each group.

And when a bar chart makes a small gap between two branches look huge, you check first whether the vertical axis starts at zero. Today we ask a harder question about numbers like these. How much can they move just because of which records we looked at?

Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The population is every record you care about. A sample is the part you actually look at. The gap between a sample statistic and the population value is sampling error. How much a statistic changes from sample to sample is sampling variability.
The standard deviation of a statistic across many samples, such as the sample mean. It says how far one sample can sit from the truth.
Many random draws done by computer to see what a statistic does. In Sheets: RAND and INDEX, filled down.
A number from -1 to +1 for how closely two numeric variables rise and fall together. Correlation is not causation.
A variable that influences both of two variables you are comparing, so they look linked. Also called a confounding variable.

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bars_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_switch_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.66.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_0.66.png

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Population and sample. The population is every record you care about. A sample is the part you actually look at. The gap between a sample statistic and the population value is sampling error. How much a statistic changes from sample to sample is sampling variability.

Standard error. The standard deviation of a statistic across many samples, such as the sample mean. It says how far one sample can sit from the truth.

Monte Carlo simulation. Many random draws done by computer to see what a statistic does. In Sheets: RAND and INDEX, filled down.

Correlation (Pearson r). A number from -1 to +1 for how closely two numeric variables rise and fall together. Correlation is not causation.

Confounder. A variable that influences both of two variables you are comparing, so they look linked. Also called a confounding variable.

title.text:
Probability is a share between 0 and 1: about
7 orders in 100 are above 100,000 UGX

objects.text: 139 of 2,000 orders are above 100,000 UGX. P(order above 100,000) = 139 ÷ 2,000 = 0.0695.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_28e725c3.png
objects.alt: Probability is a share between 0 and 1: about 7 orders in 100 are above 100,000 UGX

slides.notes:
Let us start with probability. A probability is a number between zero and one that says how likely an event is. When you can count records, it is the count of the event divided by the count of all records. In the workbook, 139 of the 2,000 orders are above 100,000 shillings.

That is 0.0695, or about 7 orders in every 100. In Sheets, COUNTIF with greater than 100000, divided by the count of orders, gives it. This is a relative frequency: a share observed in data. Does that share tell you whether the next order will be large?

title.text:
A share settles as you count
more records: this is the long run

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_settle_11.90x4.25_fe4334e9.png
objects.alt: A share settles as you count more records: this is the long run

objects.text: Early shares swing. Later shares settle. This is the law of large numbers.

slides.notes:
Here is the same share, but counted as orders arrive in a random order. After 20 orders the share swings a lot, because one or two large orders change it. As we count more, the line settles near the dashed red line, 6.95 percent. This settling is called the law of large numbers: a share measured over many records stays closer and closer to its long-run value.

In the full file of 30,229 orders the share is 7.32 percent. So the workbook share is close to it but not identical. Why do you think the two differ?

title.text:
A sample is drawn from a population, and a
statistic from the sample estimates a parameter

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_popsample_11.90x4.25_1df15fe5.png
objects.alt: A sample is drawn from a population, and a statistic from the sample estimates a parameter

objects.text: The workbook is itself a sample of the full file. Here we treat its 2,000 orders as the population.

slides.notes:
Now the key idea. A population is every record you care about. A sample is the part you actually look at. A number that describes the population is a parameter. A number computed from the sample is a statistic. For this lesson we treat the 2,000 orders in the workbook as the population.

Its mean, the parameter, is 49,931 shillings. We draw thirty orders at random, the gold dots, and compute their mean, the statistic. Our first sample gave 33,396. The difference, -16,535, is sampling error. Nobody made a mistake. It comes only from which records were drawn. The workbook is itself a sample of the full file, which is why we say we treat it as the population.

Why can we never see the true parameter in real work?

title.text:
Three random samples of 30 orders give three
different means, and the gaps are sampling error

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_folder_0.39.png

objects.text: These samples come from one seeded run of the simulation. Yours will differ. Sampling error = sample mean minus population mean.

slides.notes:
Here are three random samples of thirty orders, taken from the simulation we build in a minute. Sample 1 has a mean of 33,396, which is 16,535 below the population mean. Sample 2 has 36,610, 13,321 below. Sample 3 has 34,348, only 15,583 away. Each gap is that sample's sampling error.

Notice that all three sit well below the true mean. Because order values are right-skewed, most samples of thirty contain none of the few huge orders, and a few samples that catch one sit far above. Why would a bigger sample help?

title.text:
A Monte Carlo simulation repeats a random
draw many times: five steps in Sheets

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_0dea458c.png
objects.alt: A Monte Carlo simulation repeats a random draw many times: five steps in Sheets

objects.text: Each draw puts a random row number into INDEX. Drawing the same row twice is allowed: sampling with replacement.

slides.notes:
A Monte Carlo simulation repeats a random draw many times to see what a statistic does. In Sheets it takes five steps. One, in cell A2 draw one random order with INDEX and RAND. Two, fill right to column AD, which gives thirty random orders in one row: that row is one sample.

Three, in AE2 take the average of A2 to AD2: the sample mean. Four, fill the whole row down to row 201, so you have two hundred samples and two hundred sample means. Five, freeze the numbers by pasting values, then chart them. Each draw may pick the same row twice.

That is called sampling with replacement. Why does it matter that each draw is independent?

title.text:
Three small formulas build one
random draw and one sample mean

rows.text: A number from 0 up to just below 1, new on every recalculation
The order value in that row
One mean for the row of 30 orders

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_switch_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_pin_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_receipt_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_calculator_0.50.png

objects.text: =RANDBETWEEN(1,2000) is a shortcut for the second formula. Both can give the same row twice.

slides.notes:
Here are the formulas. RAND gives a random decimal from zero up to just below one. Multiply it by 2000, take INT to cut off the decimals, and add one, and you have a random row number from one to two thousand. INDEX uses that row number to read an order value from column G of the orders tab.

That is one random order. Fill it across thirty cells and you have a sample. AVERAGE of that row is the sample mean. RANDBETWEEN of one and two thousand is a shortcut for the row number. Only INDEX and INT are new to you. Which of these formulas would you change to draw a sample of fifty?

title.text:
RAND recalculates on every edit, so
freeze the results before you chart them

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Live formulas

runs.text: Every edit redraws all 6,000 random draws and 200 means.
Your histogram changes while you look at it.
Sheets has no setting to fix the draw.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.75.png

objects.text: Frozen values

runs.text: Copy the block, then Paste special, Values only.
The numbers stay fixed.
Now compute and chart.

objects.text: Sheets cannot fix a draw, so freeze the values.

slides.notes:
Here is the trap in every Sheets simulation. RAND recalculates every time anything changes on the sheet. Your block holds 6,000 random draws and the 200 means built on them, so a single edit redraws them all, and your histogram changes under your hands. Sheets has no way to fix the random draw.

So before you chart or compute anything, copy the block and use Paste special, Values only. Then the numbers stay put. In Excel, you can set Calculation Options to Manual instead. In Python you can set a random seed, a starting number that makes the same random numbers appear every run.

That is called reproducibility, and we meet random seeds later in the course. Which would you prefer for a report you must defend?

title.text:
200 samples of 30 orders give 200 different means:
together they form the sampling distribution

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_hist_11.90x4.25_ba370823.png
objects.alt: 200 samples of 30 orders give 200 different means: together they form the sampling distribution

objects.text: One seeded run of the exercise. Your own run will look similar but not identical.

slides.notes:
Here is what two hundred samples look like. Each bar counts samples whose mean falls in a band of ten thousand shillings. The means run from 20,069 to 142,300. They centre near the population mean, the red line: the mean of the two hundred means is 50,205. So one sample can miss by a lot, yet the samples as a group centre on the truth.

Together these 200 sample means form the sampling distribution. Their spread, measured by the standard deviation of the means, is the standard error, which comes next. This is sampling variability on the page. Notice the long tail to the right, the skewness from Session 3. And 122 of the 200 sample means sit below the population mean.

Why would more than half sit below?

title.text:
The standard error is the standard
deviation of the sample means

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.40_ba3f12e5.png
objects.alt: The standard error is the standard deviation of the sample means

rows.text: Standard error: the spread of the sample means across many samples
One value in each sample row

objects.text: With one real sample you do not know sigma, so you use s, the sample standard deviation.

slides.notes:
Here is the standard error. It is the standard deviation of the sample means, the spread of the sampling distribution. A formula gives it without simulating: the population standard deviation, sigma, divided by the square root of the sample size, n. For our orders, sigma is 128,062 and n is thirty, so the standard error is 23,381 shillings.

Our simulation of two hundred means gave a standard deviation of 22,606, which is close. In real work you only have one sample and do not know sigma, so you use the sample standard deviation instead. A smaller standard error means a more trustworthy sample mean. What would make it smaller?

title.text:
A larger sample has a smaller
standard error: quadruple n to halve it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_panels_11.90x4.25_18cf7004.png
objects.alt: A larger sample has a smaller standard error: quadruple n to halve it

objects.text: Each panel shows 200 sample means on the same scale. SE = sigma divided by the square root of n.

slides.notes:
Now the same exercise for three sample sizes. With five orders in each sample, the standard error is 57,271 and the means are spread far and wide. With thirty, it is 23,381. With two hundred it is 9,055, and the means huddle round the population mean. Because of the square root, quadrupling the sample size halves the standard error.

Going from thirty to one hundred and twenty would cut it in half. Going from five to thirty cuts it by a factor of 2.4. More data helps, but with diminishing returns. What would it cost your organisation to collect four times as many records?

title.text:
Sample means of skewed data stay skewed at
small n and become bell-shaped as n grows

rows.text: Share of samples below the population mean

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bars_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bars_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bars_0.39.png

objects.text: From 20,000 repeats of each sample size. Order values have skewness 8.76. This pattern is the central limit theorem at work.

slides.notes:
This table explains why more than half of our samples sat below the population mean. Order values are very right-skewed, with skewness 8.76. For samples of five, the sample means have skewness 3.95, and 76 percent of samples fall below the true mean. For samples of thirty the skewness is 1.63, and for two hundred it is 0.64, with 54 percent below.

As n grows, the sampling distribution gets closer to a bell shape and to symmetry. That is the central limit theorem. It works slowly when the data is heavily skewed. These figures come from twenty thousand repeats of each size. What does that tell you about a survey of thirty records?

title.text:
Correlation (Pearson r) measures how
closely two variables rise and fall together

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_scatters_11.90x4.25_1045135d.png
objects.alt: Correlation (Pearson r) measures how closely two variables rise and fall together

objects.text: Each dot is one branch in one week: 832 records from the branch_weeks tab.

slides.notes:
Correlation measures how closely two numeric variables rise and fall together. The Pearson correlation coefficient, written r, runs from minus one to plus one. Each dot here is one branch in one week. On the left, footfall and orders have r of 0.84: strongly positive, busier weeks have more orders.

In the middle, rainfall and orders have r of -0.22: weakly negative. On the right, footfall and rainfall have r of 0.00, essentially zero: no linear link. In Sheets, the function is CORREL. Which of the three pictures would you trust for a forecast?

title.text:
Pearson r multiplies how far two variables
sit from their means, record by record

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.40_2301852f.png
objects.alt: Pearson r multiplies how far two variables sit from their means, record by record

rows.text: Footfall and orders of branch-week i
The mean footfall and the mean orders
Share of the variance in orders that a straight line on footfall accounts for (coefficient of determination)

objects.text: In Sheets: =CORREL(branch_weeks!C2:C833,branch_weeks!F2:F833). Pearson r measures only straight-line association.

slides.notes:
Here is the formula. For each record, take how far footfall is above or below its mean and how far orders are above or below its mean, and multiply the two. When both are above average together, or both below, the product is positive. When one is above and the other below, it is negative.

Add the products and divide by a scaling term so the answer sits between minus one and plus one. For footfall and orders across 832 branch weeks, r is 0.84. Squared, it is 0.71, so about 71 percent of the variance in orders is accounted for by a straight line on footfall.

That is the coefficient of determination. Pearson r only measures straight-line association. Why would a curve fool it?

title.text: Reading r: size, sign and what it cannot tell you

rows.text: Strong, positive. Busier weeks have more orders. It says nothing about which causes which.
Weak, negative. Wetter weeks have somewhat fewer orders, with a lot of scatter.
Malaria cases and rain, same month, District Clinics
Near zero, yet with last month's rain r is 0.37. A delay can hide a real link.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cloud_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_sun_0.38.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clinic_0.50.png

objects.text: Cut-offs such as strong and weak are judgement, not law. Always draw the scatter plot before you trust r.

slides.notes:
Let me show you how to read r. Footfall and orders, 0.84: strong and positive, but it does not say which causes which. Rainfall and orders, -0.22: weak and negative, with a lot of scatter. Footfall and rainfall, 0.00: about zero. The last row is a warning from the District Clinics file.

Malaria cases and rainfall in the same month have r of 0.00, almost nothing. But pair each month's cases with the previous month's rain and r is 0.37. A delay can hide a real link. Words like strong and weak are judgement, so always draw the scatter plot first.

Where might a delay hide a link in your data?

title.text:
A confounder influences both
variables, so they look linked

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsb_confound_7.70x4.80_1cbcb14b.png
objects.alt: A confounder influences both variables, so they look linked

objects.text: Confounder (confounding variable): a variable that drives both of the variables you compare.

runs.text: Larger branches have more footfall and more orders.
Part of the 0.84 comes from branch size.
Correlation alone cannot show cause.

slides.notes:
Here is why correlation is not causation. A confounder is a variable that influences both of the variables you compare, so they look linked even if neither causes the other. Look at branch size. Kampala Central, size 1.6, has about 2,958 visitors and 56.6 orders a week. Fort Portal, size 0.7, has 1,310 and 26.8.

Size lifts both, which inflates the 0.84. Inside a single branch the correlation is lower, from 0.53 to 0.73. Footfall may still cause some orders, but the correlation alone cannot separate the two stories. Would flyers that raise footfall raise orders by the same amount?

both come from records that are missing

objects.text: Selection bias

runs.text: Records not chosen by chance.
Workbook means: loyalty 48,672, 580 walk-ins 53,013.
Full file: 47,432 and 47,628.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_flag_0.75.png

objects.text: Survivorship bias

runs.text: Studying only what is still there.
Hypothetical: judging a strategy only from branches that are still open.

objects.text: Ask who or what could not get into the sample.

slides.notes:
Two ways a sample misleads you. Selection bias happens when records are chosen by something other than chance. If you report only loyalty orders, you leave out 580 walk-in orders, 29 percent of the workbook. Their mean is 53,013 against 48,672, lifted by one huge walk-in order. In the full file the two means are close, 47,628 and 47,432, so here the effect is mild, but you only know that after you check.

Survivorship bias is studying only what remains. This example is hypothetical: judging a branch strategy from branches that are still open hides the ones that closed. What might be missing from a table you use at work?

runs.text: Line 1 draws one random order. Fill it right to AD for one sample of 30.
Line 2 gives the sample mean of that row. Fill down to row 201.
Line 3 is the standard error estimate from your 200 means: about 19,185 to 27,760.

Line 5 gives r for footfall and orders: 0.84.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the five formulas that do the work. Line one draws one random order. Fill it right to column AD for one sample of thirty. Line two averages that row, the sample mean, and you fill it down to row 201. Line three, STDEV of the two hundred means, estimates the standard error.

Expect a value between about 19,185 and 27,760. Line four counts how many sample means fall below the population mean. Expect between about 114 and 146. A value just outside a range is not necessarily an error: freeze a new run and check again. Line five is CORREL on the branch weeks tab.

It gives 0.84, the same for everyone because it uses no random numbers. Why do the first four differ between learners?

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: Samples of 30 give a standard error of 23,381 UGX. What happens to it with samples of 120?
It halves, to about 11,690, because it is sigma divided by the square root of n.
A manager sees r = 0.84 between footfall and orders and wants to fund flyers. What do you say?
Branch size is a confounder: it lifts both. Inside one branch r is lower. Test flyers at some branches against similar branches without.
Why is reporting only loyalty-card orders risky?
It is selection bias: the records were chosen by something other than chance, and walk-in shoppers are left out.
